analysis.one_liner: Repeals the new health care law and replaces it with incentives to buy coverage.
analysis.headline: Introduced two days after the Affordable Care Act became law, the bill was referred to ten committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe the Affordable Care Act off the books as if it had never passed, restoring the health insurance rules that existed before it, and then enact a separate Republican plan, the Empowering Patients First Act, that relies on incentives rather than requirements to encourage people to buy insurance [S2][S3]. It was filed on March 22, 2010, two days after President Obama signed the health care law, when Democrats controlled the House, the Senate, and the White House [S1]. It never got a hearing or a vote and expired when the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the law's repeal would have removed the Affordable Care Act's rules on insurers and its financing, returning health insurance to the pre-2010 legal landscape, while the replacement plan would offer incentives to encourage voluntary purchase of coverage [S2][S3]. Higher-income households and industries that bore new costs or rules under the health law would have gained most, since repeal restores the prior law wholesale [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act effective as of its own enactment and restores the provisions of law that the Act amended or repealed [S2][S3].

It then enacts the Empowering Patients First Act (H.R. 3400 from the same Congress), which the bill's title describes as providing incentives to encourage health insurance coverage rather than requiring it [S1][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who would have gained coverage or protections under the Affordable Care Act would bear the cost of repeal: the CRS summary confirms the bill undoes the Act entirely and puts back the law as it stood before [S2]. Because the replacement relies on incentives to 'encourage' coverage, people the incentives do not reach would be left where they were before 2010 [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: People the old system left uncovered

drawbacks.text: An immediate repeal would strip the Affordable Care Act's provisions all at once — the CRS summary says the Act is repealed and prior law restored as if it had never been enacted — leaving people who had come to rely on it without a transition [S2].

The replacement plan's own framing is about incentives to 'encourage' coverage, meaning insurance would remain voluntary and people with expensive conditions could again face the pre-2010 insurance market [S1][S3].
The bill is a one-section swap: it does not contain a replacement plan of its own, it simply enacts an earlier bill by reference, so voters could not see the full substitute text in this bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims at a real goal — wider access to insurance through different means — but as written it puts repeal first and the replacement second, with no transition for people already relying on the new law. An honest supporter would acknowledge that repealing first and hoping the substitute works is a bigger gamble for patients than it is for anyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced two days after the health care law was signed, got referred to ten committees and then to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Dan Burton introduced the bill on March 22, 2010, the same day it was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and nine other committees [S1][S5].
On March 29 and April 30, 2010, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Education and Labor Health Subcommittee respectively, where no further action followed [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded; the last action of the bill is the April 30 subcommittee referral, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].
Twenty-seven Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did, and with Democrats holding 253 of 435 House seats the bill never had a path to a floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Affordable Care Act's provisions remained in place; no one's insurance rules changed. The bill's supporters got a recorded position but no change in law, and the concentrated interests that would have benefited from repeal gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People covered by the new health law

for.name: Dan Burton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 22, 2010, two days after the Affordable Care Act was signed into law.

against.name: House Democratic majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor (253 of 435 seats)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote during the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on March 29, 2010, and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; with Democrats holding the House majority and the White House, no Democratic support is recorded and the bill never reached the floor [S4][S5].

industries.note: Repeal would remove the health law's new rules on insurers but also the mandate structure that steered millions of new subsidized customers to them, so the industry's gains and losses pull both ways [S2]. Its interest in rolling back consumer-facing regulation runs against the people the law was written to protect.

The Affordable Care Act was financed in part by taxes that fell more heavily on higher incomes; a full repeal restores prior law and removes those obligations, which ordinary taxpayers would not share in equally [S2].
